Compute goodness-of-fit metrics for a fitted model

Source: R/model-classes.R
model_metrics.Rd

Reports RMSE, MAE, MAPE, SMAPE, \(R^2\) and adjusted \(R^2\) for any spatial_fit as a one-row data frame. With newdata it scores rows you held out yourself. Without it, it reads the fit's own fitted values: in-sample for a GWR or a Bayesian GP fit, out-of-bag for a random forest. Those numbers do not compare across backends, and the data frame carries no label saying which kind it holds.

Usage

model_metrics(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'spatial_fit'
model_metrics(object, newdata = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

A spatial_fit object.

...

Passed to predict() when newdata is given. Without newdata nothing reads them, so any argument here is an error, which catches a misspelt newdata. The metrics are computed from one predicted value per row, so draws = TRUE (a Bayesian GP fit) and se.fit = TRUE (a GWR fit), with which predict() returns a matrix or a list, are refused.

newdata

Optional sf object of held-out rows, carrying the response and the predictors. If NULL, the fitted values are used (in-sample, or out-of-bag for an rf_fit; see "What the metrics are computed on").

Value

A one-row data.frame with n, RMSE, MAE, MAPE, SMAPE, R2, Adj_R2, n_MAPE and n_SMAPE (the last two are the rows each percentage error was averaged over). Adj_R2 is always NA: a GWR's effective number of parameters far exceeds the global predictor count and a GP model has no simple p. A character or factor response is an error; a logical response is scored as 0/1.

Details

Use this function for one fit. evaluate_insample() runs it over a list of fits and labels each row with its basis, and compare_models() adds information criteria and residual Moran's I to that table. None of the three refits a model. An in-sample score is not a cross-validation score: a GWR can reach a near-perfect in-sample \(R^2\) at a small bandwidth without predicting anything. For a figure you can report, use cv_gwr(), cv_bayes(), cv_rf() or compare_models_cv().

What the metrics are computed on

With newdata = NULL the metrics come from fitted(object). That is in-sample for a GWR or a Bayesian GP fit, and out-of-bag for a random forest, whose fitted() method returns out-of-bag predictions (see fit_rf_model()). Check object$info$fitted_are_oob before comparing numbers across backends; evaluate_insample() and compare_models() record it per model in a metric_basis column, and compare_models_cv() scores every backend the same way.

\(R^2\) is \(1 - RSS/TSS\) with the total sum of squares taken about the mean of the response the model was fitted to. In sample that is the ordinary \(R^2\). With newdata it is the out-of-sample \(R^2\) every cv_*() function uses: the model is measured against the training mean, the prediction it had to beat, and not against the new rows' own mean, which it could not have known. It is below 0 when the model predicts the new rows worse than the training mean does, and NA when the response does not vary about that mean beyond the rounding of its values, whatever its units and origin.

A GWR fit whose response fit_gwr_model() took about a centre (fit$engine$centres$response, a response at a large offset) is scored on the response and the fitted values or predictions less that centre, which keep digits that rounding at the response's size would lose: RMSE, MAE and \(R^2\) are those of the same values at 0, and MAPE and SMAPE divide the same errors by the values in the response's units. fitted() and predict() still return values in the response's units.

Percentage errors on responses with zeros

MAPE divides by the observed value and SMAPE by \(|y| + |\hat{y}|\), so neither is defined where its denominator is zero. Neither returns Inf or NaN. Both are averaged over the rows whose denominator is non-zero, and are NA when no row qualifies. Non-zero is judged at the scale of the data: a denominator no larger than 100 machine epsilons times the largest one counts as zero, so the rule does not depend on the units of the response. The n_MAPE and n_SMAPE columns record how many rows that was; the n column (n_pred in a cross-validation result) counts finite observation/prediction pairs. Read a percentage error next to that count: when n_MAPE is smaller, MAPE is an average over a subset of the data, whatever its value.

Any response taking exact zeros is affected: counts, rainfall, abundance, claim amounts. On a zero-inflated response with 62 zeros out of 120, MAPE averages the 58 non-zero rows and n_MAPE is 58. SMAPE drops the rows where observation and prediction are both near zero, which on a well-fitted zero-inflated model are the rows it got right, so it averages the harder rows only and reads worse than the fit deserves. n_SMAPE shows how many rows it kept; it does not correct the average.

RMSE, MAE and \(R^2\) use every finite row; prefer them whenever the response can be zero. For a Bayesian GP fit, cv_bayes() also reports CRPS and interval coverage, which are proper scoring rules and are defined at zero.

Which metrics survive a non-Gaussian response

RMSE and MAE are defined for any numeric response and are what to read for a count, a rate or a bounded outcome. MAPE and SMAPE assume a response that is rarely zero (see "Percentage errors on responses with zeros"), and \(R^2\) and adjusted \(R^2\) compare residual variance to total variance, which suits a Gaussian response and fits loosely anything whose variance tracks its mean. On a Poisson or zero-inflated response read the four as a rough summary rather than a score.

For the Bayesian GP, cv_bayes() also reports CRPS and interval coverage at its coverage_levels (50, 80 and 95 percent by default). Both are proper scoring rules computed from posterior draws, so they are meaningful for any family that predicts one number per row (a count, a rate, a binary or bounded outcome), and they are the numbers to compare when the response is not Gaussian. A categorical or ordinal family predicts a probability per response category instead, so cv_bayes() refuses one before fitting anything. When every fold fails, the fold_metrics frame cv_bayes() returns carries the CRPS column but not the coverage_* columns, so code that reads those columns must allow for their absence.

See also

Other in-sample checks: compare_models(), evaluate_insample(), print.morans_i(), residual_morans_i()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(60, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(60, 0, 1000),
             a = rnorm(60)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
# An offset keeps the response away from zero, where MAPE is undefined.
pts$z <- 10 + 2 * pts$a + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3)
# Fit on 40 rows and keep 20 back, so the second call is out of sample.
fit <- fit_rf_model(pts[1:40, ], "z", "a", num_trees = 50, seed = 1)
model_metrics(fit)                           # out-of-bag for a forest
#>    n     RMSE       MAE     MAPE    SMAPE        R2 Adj_R2 n_MAPE n_SMAPE
#> 1 40 0.409009 0.3236812 3.425689 3.390414 0.9541711     NA     40      40
model_metrics(fit, newdata = pts[41:60, ])   # on the 20 held-out rows
#>    n      RMSE       MAE    MAPE    SMAPE        R2 Adj_R2 n_MAPE n_SMAPE
#> 1 20 0.5080838 0.3836504 3.56621 3.649174 0.9022065     NA     20      20
